Local AWS sandbox
=================

This box has no route to AWS. Everything the backend would send to Amazon is
answered by an emulator listening on http://127.0.0.1:4566, which speaks the
same wire protocols the AWS SDK uses. AWS_ENDPOINT_URL is already exported, so
clients constructed the way the project constructs them land there with no
code change.

The credentials in the environment belong to the platform account that holds
the datastore measurement buckets:

    account            900000000001
    region             us-east-1
    businesses seen    biz-cadence, biz-lumen

The two buckets this deployment was configured with are named by the
environment, not by the code, and the verifier runs against a different pair:

    DB_MEASUREMENT_BUCKET_NAME       where customers' usage files are dropped
    DB_MEASUREMENT_DLQ_BUCKET_NAME   where intake failures are kept

The second one is not empty. It holds what earlier failures of this deployment
left behind, from a period when the intake still kept them, and it is the only
surviving description of how those records were written.

The world the emulator is currently serving is described by
/opt/dlq-sandbox/public.json. It is small and quiet: a few source files and a
handful of past failures. Real deployments run far more traffic through the
same two buckets, so treat what you see here as a sample rather than the shape
of the world.

To point the emulator at a different world, restart it yourself:

Local AWS sandbox
=================

This box has no route to AWS. Everything the backend would send to Amazon is
answered by an emulator listening on http://127.0.0.1:4566, which speaks the
same wire protocols the AWS SDK uses. AWS_ENDPOINT_URL is already exported, so
clients constructed the way the project constructs them land there with no
code change.

The credentials in the environment belong to the platform account that holds
the datastore measurement buckets:

    account            900000000001
    region             us-east-1
    businesses seen    biz-cadence, biz-lumen

The two buckets this deployment was configured with are named by the
environment, not by the code, and the verifier runs against a different pair:

    DB_MEASUREMENT_BUCKET_NAME       where customers' usage files are dropped
    DB_MEASUREMENT_DLQ_BUCKET_NAME   where intake failures are kept

The second one is not empty. It holds what earlier failures of this deployment
left behind, from a period when the intake still kept them, and it is the only
surviving description of how those records were written.

The world the emulator is currently serving is described by
/opt/dlq-sandbox/public.json. It is small and quiet: a few source files and a
handful of past failures. Real deployments run far more traffic through the
same two buckets, so treat what you see here as a sample rather than the shape
of the world.

To point the emulator at a different world, restart it yourself:

    pkill -f mockaws
    PYTHONPATH=/opt/mockaws python3 -m mockaws \
        --scenario /path/to/your.json --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4566 --seed 7 &

That is also how to see what the intake does when a bucket it expects is not
there: write a world without one and point the emulator at it.

TypeScript in this project can be run directly with tsx, for example

    tsx -e "import('./src/usage/usage.controller.js').then(console.log)"

and the buckets answer an ordinary S3 client, or plain HTTP:

    curl -s "$AWS_ENDPOINT_URL/$DB_MEASUREMENT_DLQ_BUCKET_NAME?list-type=2"
